source.title: Scaling Sparse and Dense Retrieval in Decoder-Only LLMs
source.authors: Hansi Zeng; J. Killingback; Hamed Zamani

record.file_problem: Full paper text and appendix are present. The supplied text omits the plotted data in Figure 1, so its individual values cannot be extracted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream retrieval-performance scaling across Llama 3 sizes and training objectives, using ranking metrics rather than held-out cross-entropy or the original language-model scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports retrieval metrics by model size and objective in Tables 2 and 3, which bear on V6. Figure 1 is also described qualitatively, but its plotted values are not present in the supplied text. The paper does not measure pretraining cross-entropy, fit loss power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or find compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: The study reports downstream retrieval metrics (MRR@10, nDCG@10) for Llama 3 1B, 3B and 8B backbones after retrieval fine-tuning. That is a new setting with a result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It fits no curve, measures no pretraining loss, and has only three sizes, so T3 fits better than T2. Model size is confounded with training amount: compute is fixed, so larger models train fewer epochs (CL: 7/3/1; KD: 56/24/8, Table 5).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Scaling gains appear clearly only with CL. KD models perform similarly across 1B–8B, and dense-KD declines on BEIR at larger scales. Sparse retrieval outperforms dense, especially out of domain. CL+KD gives the best trade-off, and Lion-SP-8B reaches state-of-the-art results. The authors hypothesise that large students may surpass the cross-encoder teacher.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies fine-tuned retrieval performance (MRR@10 and nDCG@10), not held-out language-model cross-entropy. It compares Llama 3 1B, 3B, and 8B retrieval systems under a fixed fine-tuning compute budget and varies retrieval paradigm and objective; it does not fit language-model scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling outcomes differ by fine-tuning objective (CL versus KD versus CL + KD), retrieval paradigm (sparse versus dense), and evaluation domain. Training configurations vary by model size and objective.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (2025); the supplied paper text also contains placeholder conference/citation boilerplate.
record.problems: Only three model sizes (1B, 3B, 8B) are evaluated, and the study uses retrieval metrics rather than pretraining loss. It uses a single teacher model, noted by the authors as a limitation. The supplied text does not include Figure 1's plotted values. Tables 2 and 3 give no uncertainty estimates for the scaling comparisons; significance testing is reported for baseline comparisons in Table 4, not these scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1's qualitative trends are not added as separate rows because the supplied text omits the plotted values and the table rows record the available objective-by-size metrics. Table 4 baseline-comparison results are omitted because those comparisons do not add a separate model-size scaling measurement beyond the reported retrieval results.

untested.parts: Predictability: no fitted relationship and only three sizes. No link between downstream performance and pretraining loss. The effect of size is not isolated from training epochs under the fixed compute budget.
Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form is fitted for fine-tuning or retrieval.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: CL-only and KD-only results by size on in-domain TREC DL 19+20 (and BEIR). The text says CL rises significantly in-domain, while 1B and 8B KD 'perform similarly' in-domain. The values are only plotted.
Training amount varies with size under the fixed compute budget (epochs 7/3/1 for CL, 56/24/8 for KD). This should be recorded as a condition on every scaling row.

record.verdict_notes: The T3 CL+KD BEIR rows duplicate the T2 BEIR rows. Table 3 parentheticals are gaps to teacher reranking, not scaling baselines. Table 4 compares the study's own method with baselines and is correctly left out. Llama 3 1B/3B backbones differ from 8B in pretraining provenance, a further confound the paper does not address.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on smaller runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their scaling with compute; a fixed fine-tuning compute budget is used, but no optimum is sought.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms across other modalities or the specified training regimes.
The paper measures retrieval metrics after retrieval fine-tuning, not downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; it does not fit a predictive relationship.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting choices, and departures from a single fitted power law are not measured. The paper does compare retrieval scaling across fine-tuning objectives.

relationships.condition: CL-trained sparse and dense retrievers, BEIR, and (per the text on Figure 1) in-domain TREC DL
relationships.reason: BEIR nDCG@10 rises monotonically 1B→8B: sparse .496/.528/.557, dense .435/.491/.534 (T3-S-CL-*, T3-D-CL-*). The text says CL in-domain performance 'increases significantly' too, but that is not in the rows.
relationships.display_finding: BEIR nDCG@10 increased from 0.496 through 0.528 to 0.557 for sparse retrieval and from 0.435 through 0.491 to 0.534 for dense retrieval, with significant in-domain gains also reported.

source_check.reason: Table 3 gives monotonic BEIR gains for sparse CL (.496/.528/.557) and dense CL (.435/.491/.534); Section 3 explicitly reports significant in-domain gains with CL.

relationships.condition: Sparse KD and sparse CL+KD on all sets, and dense CL+KD in-domain
relationships.reason: Gains are small or plateau. Sparse KD BEIR goes .517→.536. Sparse CL+KD MSMARCO goes .410→.417→.417. Dense CL+KD TREC goes .749→.760→.757. The authors call KD scaling minimal.
relationships.display_finding: Sparse KD BEIR rose from 0.517 to 0.536, sparse CL+KD MSMARCO plateaued at 0.417 after 0.410, and dense CL+KD TREC changed from 0.749 to 0.760 to 0.757.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Sparse KD and sparse CL+KD on all sets, and dense CL+KD in-domain
source_check.reason: Sparse KD gains are small; sparse CL+KD improves modestly or plateaus; dense CL+KD shows modest MSMARCO gains and nonmonotonic TREC scores. These results qualify the scaling benefit.

relationships.condition: Dense retrievers trained with KD or CL+KD, out-of-domain BEIR
relationships.reason: There is no improvement with size. Dense KD goes .489→.477→.485 (below 1B at 8B). Dense CL+KD goes .500→.496→.501. The authors attribute this to overfitting to the teacher. Size is confounded with fewer epochs.
relationships.display_finding: Dense KD scores were 0.489→0.477→0.485 and CL+KD scores were 0.500→0.496→0.501, with teacher overfitting proposed as an explanation and fewer epochs confounding size.
